newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Britain warns Serbs over Bosnia presidency boycott.
newsitem.headline: Britain warns Serbs over Bosnia presidency boycott.

text.p: Britain on Thursday warned the Bosnian Serbs they risked losing international financial support if they continued to refuse to cooperate with the newly-elected Bosnian presidency.

Foreign Office minister Sir Nicholas Bonsor said he told Bosnian Serb presidency member Momcilo Krajisnik of the importance of the country's three-man presidency and its joint national assembly, whose inaugural session in Sarajevo last Saturday the Serbs had boycotted.

"It will be very difficult for the international community to continue to assist with finance and resources unless we have the full cooperation of all three groups in Bosnia," Bonsor told a Sarajevo news conference.

"I made it clear to him that unless the presidency progresses and unless the Republika Srpska (Bosnian Serb) representatives do cooperate fully in the process of getting this government in place then clearly the funds which the World Bank and other international institutions have set aside for them will not be forthcoming," he said.
Bonsor, on a three-day visit to Bosnia, said Krajisnik had "fully accepted the point" and would do everything in his power to ensure that the assembly did meet as soon as possible.

Krajisnik and the Serb deputies stayed away from the first National Assembly session on Saturday, arguing that there were insufficient guarantees for their safety, and objecting to an oath of alliegence to the Bosnian constitution.
In a statement to the Bosnian Serb news agency SRNA, Krajisnik confirmed that he and the Serb deputies in the National Assembly were now ready to meet and sign the oath.
SRNA said he also called for an immediate meeting of the presidency.

"As regards the signing of a solemn oath, I have pledged to do my duty, and I said that, if this is possible and if it fits in with Mr Bildt's activities, we are ready to summon our deputies so that they might sign the oath as soon as possible," SRNA quoted Krajisnik as saying.
Krajisnik's refusal to cooperate with the National Assembly that emerged from Bosnia's first post-war elections on September 14 infuriated the international community.

But international officials in Sarajevo said on Thursday they had received indications that Krajisnik and the Serb deputies were now ready to join in the National Assembly, although they did not say when this might happen.

Colum Murphy, spokesman for Carl Bildt, the international community's High Representative in Bosnia, said: "The Bosnian Serbs painted themselves into a corner on Saturday. Now they are painting themselves out of a corner."
But if Krajisnik now appears more conciliatory, other members of the Bosnian Serb leadership remain wedded to a hardline stance.

Bosnian Serb President Biljana Plavsic has told the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe, the body charged with supervising Bosnian elections, that the Serbs could call their own local elections according to their own rules.

The head of the OSCE mission to Bosnia, Robert Frowick, has held a series of crisis meetings with leading Serbs, but his spokesman declined on Thursday to comment on Plavsic's letter to Frowick outlining her plans to hold the election without OSCE supervision.
Local elections are due on November 23 and Bonsor, who will meet Plavsic on Friday, indicated that this might be premature.

"I think there are very good arguments both for and against having those elections in November and there are legitimate reasons why some people think it better to put them off. But it is for Mr Frowick to make that decision."
